entry.title: Tanpa Disadari, Kita adalah Seorang ‘Ahli Optimasi’ di Kehidupan Sehari-hari

link.title: Tanpa Disadari, Kita adalah Seorang ‘Ahli Optimasi’ di Kehidupan Sehari-hari

entry.content:
Seri: Optimasi di Teknik Industri, Hari #1. Topik 1.1: What and Where Do We Optimize? · Read in English

Pada kehidupan sehari-hari, kita sering dihadapkan pada beberapa pilihan. Tidak jarang pilihan ini membuat kita bingung dalam mengambil keputusan. Contoh, ketika ingin membeli rumah, kita dihadapkan pada pilihan rumah yang luas tetapi jauh dari tempat kerja, atau rumah yang mungil tetapi dekat dengan pusat kota. Tentu saja, keputusan ini dipersulit dengan ketersediaan dana yang kita miliki. Atau contoh lain, ketika memilih kendaraan, kita harus menimbang antara harga unit, tingkat penggunaan bahan bakar apakah boros atau tidak, kenyamanan, serta after-sales service.

Hal serupa juga terjadi saat kita memilih makanan, pakaian, laptop, profesi, hingga kota tempat tinggal. Secara alami, kita tentu selalu menginginkan pilihan yang paling baik. Namun, karena adanya keterbatasan sumber daya dan berbagai batasan (constraints), kita tidak selalu bisa mendapatkan yang terbaik dalam segala aspek. Sebagai gantinya, kita memilih opsi yang paling optimal, yaitu keputusan terbaik yang paling masuk akal dengan mempertimbangkan prioritas, sumber daya, dan batasan yang ada. Proses inilah yang disebut sebagai optimasi.

Memahami “Pengorbanan” Lewat Desain Kendaraan

Dalam sudut pandang rekayasa (engineering), optimasi juga dapat dipahami sebagai cara kita menentukan “biaya” atau pengorbanan apa yang bersedia kita tanggung demi memperoleh manfaat yang diharapkan. Kita bisa melihat contoh nyatanya pada bagaimana para insinyur merancang berbagai jenis mobil di industri otomotif:

  • Mobil Sport (Sports Car): Jika tujuannya adalah memaksimalkan akselerasi, maka perancang perlu memaksimalkan tenaga mesin sekaligus meminimalkan bobot kendaraan dengan ukuran bodi yang ringkas. Konsekuensinya, pengemudi harus menerima pengorbanan berupa konsumsi bahan bakar yang boros dan biaya perawatan yang tinggi.
  • Mobil Hemat Bahan Bakar: Sebaliknya, untuk meminimalkan konsumsi bahan bakar, mobil umumnya dirancang berukuran kecil dengan mesin berdaya rendah, sehingga akselerasinya tidak secepat mobil sport.
  • Mobil Keluarga (Family Car): Pada jenis ini, perancang berusaha menjaga keseimbangan antara akselerasi dan efisiensi bahan bakar, sembari memenuhi batasan wajib berupa kapasitas angkut penumpang yang banyak, misalnya harus mengakomodasi tiga baris kursi.
  • Truk Kargo: Truk dibekali mesin yang sangat bertenaga untuk mengangkut beban berat, tetapi karena ukurannya yang besar, akselerasinya menjadi yang paling rendah di jalan raya.

Lalu, muncul pertanyaan menarik: mungkinkah kita membuat truk kargo yang memiliki akselerasi secepat mobil sport? Secara teknis, hal itu sangat mungkin dilakukan dengan memasang mesin berukuran raksasa. Namun, pabrikan tidak melakukannya karena berdasarkan perhitungan, biaya produksinya akan sangat mahal dan volume penjualannya bakal rendah. Artinya, keputusan tersebut tidak optimal secara ekonomi maupun teknis.

Di sisi konsumen, pola pikir optimasi yang sama juga berlaku. Ada orang-orang yang memilih untuk tidak mengalokasikan terlalu banyak dana pada pembelian mobil, agar sisa sumber daya finansialnya bisa digunakan untuk kebutuhan lain yang dianggap lebih penting atau lebih mereka nikmati.

Membawa Persoalan Nyata ke dalam Model Matematika

Di bidang Teknik Industri dan Manajemen, prinsip optimasi menjadi fondasi utama dalam pengambilan keputusan. Misalnya, bagaimana meminimalkan biaya produksi suatu barang tanpa mengurangi standar kualitas yang ditetapkan, bagaimana memaksimalkan keuntungan perusahaan di bawah keterbatasan anggaran, atau bagaimana mengatur pembagian tugas karyawan secara efisien.

Agar persoalan-persoalan nyata tersebut dapat diselesaikan secara sistematis, kita perlu menerjemahkannya ke dalam bahasa matematika. Proses ini disebut sebagai pemodelan (modeling). Secara garis besar, setiap model optimasi terdiri dari tiga elemen utama:

  1. Variabel Keputusan (Decision Variables): Faktor atau nilai yang dapat kita atur dan tentukan besarannya (misalnya x₁, x₂, …, xₙ), seperti kapasitas mesin atau jumlah unit yang dipesan.
  2. Fungsi Tujuan (Objective Function): Ukuran kinerja utama f(x) yang ingin kita maksimalkan (seperti keuntungan atau akselerasi) atau minimalkan (seperti biaya produksi atau waktu tunggu), yang nilainya dipengaruhi oleh variabel keputusan.
  3. Batasan (Constraints): Kondisi atau aturan main yang membatasi ruang gerak keputusan kita, misalnya batas anggaran, kapasitas gudang, atau jumlah kursi penumpang.
flowchart LR
  A["Variabel Keputusan<br/>(Decision Variables)<br/>Faktor yang dapat diatur"] --> B["Fungsi Tujuan<br/>(Objective Function)<br/>Maksimalkan / Minimalkan"]
  C["Batasan<br/>(Constraints)<br/>Anggaran, Kapasitas, Aturan"] --> B
  B --> D["Solusi Optimal<br/>(Optimal Decision)<br/>Kombinasi nilai terbaik"]

Tujuan dari metode optimasi bukan hanya mencari berapa nilai maksimum atau minimum dari fungsi tujuan tersebut, melainkan menemukan kombinasi nilai variabel keputusan yang menghasilkan kondisi paling optimal. Pada pembahasan-pembahasan berikutnya, kita akan mengenal lebih jauh berbagai karakteristik masalah optimasi, mulai dari yang bersifat linear hingga non-linear, cembung (convex) hingga non-cembung, serta yang memiliki satu titik optimal (unimodal) maupun banyak titik optimal lokal (multimodal), dengan pendekatan yang bertahap dan mudah dipahami.

Referensi

Cuevas, E., Rosas Caro, J. C., Alejo Reyes, A., González Ayala, P., & Rodriguez, A. (2025). Optimization in Industrial Engineering: From Classical Methods to Modern Metaheuristics with MATLAB Applications (Chapter 1, Section 1.1: What and Where Do We Optimize, pp. 1–3). Springer Nature.
entry.summary: Optimasi di Teknik Industri, Hari #1: apa dan di mana kita melakukan optimasi?

entry.title: Without Realizing It, We Are ‘Optimization Experts’ in Everyday Life

link.title: Without Realizing It, We Are ‘Optimization Experts’ in Everyday Life

entry.content:
Series: Optimization in Industrial Engineering, Day #1. Topic 1.1: What and Where Do We Optimize? · Baca dalam Bahasa Indonesia

In our daily lives, we are frequently faced with multiple choices. Quite often, these choices make it difficult for us to reach a decision. For example, when we want to buy a house, we might be torn between a spacious home that is far from our workplace, or a smaller house located right near the city center. Of course, this decision is further complicated by the funds we have available. Another example is when we choose a vehicle: we have to weigh the purchase price, fuel consumption efficiency, driving comfort, and after-sales service.

The same pattern appears when we select food, clothing, computers, a career, or even a city to live in. Naturally, we always prefer the best possible options. However, because we constantly operate under limited resources and constraints, we cannot always get the absolute best in every single aspect. Instead, we settle on the optimal option: the best decision we can make after carefully weighing our priorities, resources, and constraints. This everyday decision-making process is what we call optimization.

Understanding “Trade-Offs” Through Vehicle Design

From an engineering standpoint, optimization can also be understood as deciding what cost or sacrifice we are willing to accept in order to obtain a desired benefit. We can see clear evidence of this in how automotive engineers design different types of vehicles:

  • Sports Cars: When the goal is to maximize acceleration, designers need to maximize engine power while minimizing vehicle weight through a compact body. The trade-off is that drivers accept higher fuel consumption and more expensive maintenance.
  • Fuel-Efficient Cars: Conversely, to minimize fuel consumption, cars are typically built smaller with low-power engines, sacrificing high acceleration in the process.
  • Large Family Cars: Here, engineers aim to maintain a balance between acceleration and fuel economy while meeting a strict constraint: carrying multiple passengers, often requiring three rows of seats.
  • Cargo Trucks: Trucks are equipped with very powerful engines to haul heavy cargo, yet because of their massive size, they end up with the lowest acceleration in practice.

This raises an interesting question: would it be possible to design a cargo truck with the acceleration of a sports car? Technically, yes, by manufacturing an enormous engine. However, manufacturers choose not to do this because their calculations show that production costs would be far too high and sales volume would be low. Simply put, such a design would not be optimal.

On the consumer side, the exact same optimization logic applies. Many people intentionally avoid spending too much of their budget on a car so they can allocate those financial resources toward other expenses they consider more important or enjoyable.

Translating Real-World Problems into Mathematical Models

In Industrial Engineering and Management, optimization serves as a core tool for strategic decision-making. Common examples include minimizing the production cost of a product while maintaining a specific quality level, maximizing company profits under budget constraints, or allocating employees to different tasks as efficiently as possible.

To solve these physical, real-world situations systematically, we first need to express them in mathematical terms, a process known as modeling. In general, every optimization model consists of three main components:

  1. Decision Variables: The independent inputs we can control or adjust (such as x₁, x₂, …, xₙ), like engine size or order quantity.
  2. Objective Function: The primary performance measure f(x) we want to maximize (such as profit or acceleration) or minimize (such as cost or waiting time), which depends on our decision variables.
  3. Constraints: The real-world limitations or conditions that bound our decisions, such as budget caps, storage capacity, or seating requirements.
flowchart LR
  A["Decision Variables<br/>(x₁, x₂, …, xₙ)<br/>Factors we can control"] --> B["Objective Function<br/>f(x)<br/>Maximize / Minimize"]
  C["Constraints<br/>Budget, capacity, rules"] --> B
  B --> D["Optimal Decision<br/>Best combination of values"]

The goal of an optimization algorithm is not merely to find the minimum or maximum value of the objective function, but to determine the exact values of the decision variables that produce that optimal outcome. As we move forward in this series, we will gradually explore different types of optimization problems, ranging from linear to nonlinear, convex to non-convex, and single-peak (unimodal) to multi-peak (multimodal), in a clear and approachable manner.

Reference

Cuevas, E., Rosas Caro, J. C., Alejo Reyes, A., González Ayala, P., & Rodriguez, A. (2025). Optimization in Industrial Engineering: From Classical Methods to Modern Metaheuristics with MATLAB Applications (Chapter 1, Section 1.1: What and Where Do We Optimize, pp. 1–3). Springer Nature.
entry.summary: Optimization in Industrial Engineering, Day #1: what and where do we optimize?

entry.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

link.title: Google Gemini updates: Flash 1.5, Gemma 2 and Project Astra

entry.content:
Gemini breaks new ground with a faster model, longer context, AI agents and moreLearn more:Learn more:Learn more:Models & ResearchProductsInfrastructure & cloudTechnology Learn more: ProductsPlatformsDevices Learn more: Outreach & initiativesLeadershipInside Google Learn more: May 14, 2024 We’re introducing a series of updates across the Gemini family of models, including the new 1.5 Flash, our lightweight model for speed and efficiency, and Project Astra, our vision for the future of AI assistants. Demis HassabisCEO of Google DeepMind, on behalf of the Gemini teamIn December, we launched our first natively multimodal model Gemini 1.0 in three sizes: Ultra, Pro and Nano. Just a few months later we released 1.5 Pro, with enhanced performance and a breakthrough long context window of 1 million tokens.Developers and enterprise customers have been putting 1.5 Pro to use in incredible ways and finding its long context window, multimodal reasoning capabilities and impressive overall performance incredibly useful.We know from user feedback that some applications need lower latency and a lower cost to serve. This inspired us to keep innovating, so today, we’re introducing Gemini 1.5 Flash: a model that’s lighter-weight than 1.5 Pro, and designed to be fast and efficient to serve at scale.Both 1.5 Pro and 1.5 Flash are available in public preview with a 1 million token context window in Google AI Studio and Vertex AI. And now, 1.5 Pro is also available with a 2 million token context window via waitlist to developers using the API and to Google Cloud customers.We’re also introducing updates across the Gemini family of models, announcing our next generation of open models, Gemma 2, and sharing progress on the future of AI assistants, with Project Astra.Context lengths of leading foundation models compared with Gemini 1.5’s 2 million token capability1.5 Flash is the newest addition to the Gemini model family and the fastest Gemini model served in the API. It’s optimized for high-volume, high-frequency tasks at scale, is more cost-efficient to serve and features our breakthrough long context window.While it’s a lighter weight model than 1.5 Pro, it’s highly capable of multimodal reasoning across vast amounts of information and delivers impressive quality for its size.The new Gemini 1.5 Flash model is optimized for speed and efficiency, is highly capable of multimodal reasoning and features our breakthrough long context window.1.5 Flash excels at summarization, chat applications, image and video captioning, data extraction from long documents and tables, and more. This is because it’s been trained by 1.5 Pro through a process called “distillation,” where the most essential knowledge and skills from a larger model are transferred to a smaller, more efficient model.Read more about 1.5 Flash in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report, on the Gemini technology page, and learn about 1.5 Flash’s availability and pricing.Over the last few months, we’ve significantly improved 1.5 Pro, our best model for general performance across a wide range of tasks.Beyond extending its context window to 2 million tokens, we’ve enhanced its code generation, logical reasoning and planning, multi-turn conversation, and audio and image understanding through data and algorithmic advances. We see strong improvements on public and internal benchmarks for each of these tasks.1.5 Pro can now follow increasingly complex and nuanced instructions, including ones that specify product-level behavior involving role, format and style. We’ve improved control over the model’s responses for specific use cases, like crafting the persona and response style of a chat agent or automating workflows through multiple function calls. And we’ve enabled users to steer model behavior by setting system instructions.We added audio understanding in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, so 1.5 Pro can now reason across image and audio for videos uploaded in Google AI Studio. And we’re now integrating 1.5 Pro into Google products, including Gemini Advanced and in Workspace apps.Read more about 1.5 Pro in our updated Gemini 1.5 technical report and on the Gemini technology page.Gemini Nano is expanding beyond text-only inputs to include images as well. Starting with Pixel, applications using Gemini Nano with Multimodality will be able to understand the world the way people do — not just through text, but also through sight, sound and spoken language.Read more about Gemini 1.0 Nano on Android.Today, we’re also sharing a series of updates to Gemma, our family of open models built from the same research and technology used to create the Gemini models.We’re announcing Gemma 2, our next generation of open models for responsible AI innovation. Gemma 2 has a new architecture designed for breakthrough performance and efficiency, and will be available in new sizes.The Gemma family is also expanding with PaliGemma, our first vision-language model inspired by PaLI-3. And we’ve upgraded our Responsible Generative AI Toolkit with LLM Comparator for evaluating the quality of model responses.Read more on the Developer blog.As part of Google DeepMind’s mission to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity, we’ve always wanted to develop universal AI agents that can be helpful in everyday life. That’s why today, we’re sharing our progress in building the future of AI assistants with Project Astra (advanced seeing and talking responsive agent).To be truly useful, an agent needs to understand and respond to the complex and dynamic world just like people do — and take in and remember what it sees and hears to understand context and take action. It also needs to be proactive, teachable and personal, so users can talk to it naturally and without lag or delay.While we’ve made incredible progress developing AI systems that can understand multimodal information, getting response time down to something conversational is a difficult engineering challenge. Over the past few years, we’ve been working to improve how our models perceive, reason and converse to make the pace and quality of interaction feel more natural.Building on Gemini, we’ve developed prototype agents that can process information faster by continuously encoding video frames, combining the video and speech input into a timeline of events, and caching this information for efficient recall.By leveraging our leading speech models, we also enhanced how they sound, giving the agents a wider range of intonations. These agents can better understand the context they’re being used in, and respond quickly, in conversation.With technology like this, it’s easy to envision a future where people could have an expert AI assistant by their side, through a phone or glasses. And some of these capabilities are coming to Google products, like the Gemini app and web experience, later this year.We’ve made incredible progress so far with our family of Gemini models, and we’re always striving to advance the state-of-the-art even further. By investing in a relentless production line of innovation, we’re able to explore new ideas at the frontier, while also unlocking the possibility of new and exciting Gemini use cases.Learn more about Gemini and its capabilities.Collection Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. entry.title: Displaying External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

link.title: Displaying External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

entry.content:
External Posts on Your al-folio Blog

If you prefer publishing blog posts on medium.com or other external sources, starting version v0.5.0, al-folio lets you to display your external posts in the blog feed of your website! 🎉🎉

Configuring external sources of super simple. After upgrading to v0.5.0, just add the following section to your _config.yml:

external_sources:
  - name: medium.com  # name of the source (arbitrary string)
    rss_url: https://medium.com/@<your-medium-username>/feed

The example above adds your medium.com blog post feed as an external source. But you can add arbitrary RSS feeds as sources.

Any questions or suggestions? 👉 Start a discussion on GitHub!
